text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London reversed from earlier uptrend to finish lower on trade and speculative profit-taking but renewed roaster buying at the lows helped slow the fall. Fresh falls in New York also provided further selling impetus. There were no market-moving news but traders noted news rains helping the Brazilian crop and that Mexico and Colombia were seeking to significantly raise production in the coming years. March finished $20 down at $1,520 a tonne, while May gave up $24 to close at $1,536 a tonne. Looking ahead, traders said the market, shadowing New York, is expected to remain volatile with prices fluctuating between $1,450 and $1,700 a tonne basis May. But robusta's downside potential will be underpinned by industry buying on the back of its hefty differential to arabicas. Traders said the real key is the size of Brazil's 1997/98 crop which will provide the market direction. BRAZIL - Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop is expected to reach between 19.7 and 22.5 million 60-kg bags, according to the first estimate from Unicafe, Brazil's leading exporter. Of this, between 1.36 and 15.6 million bags will be Group I coffee, 2.2 million to 2.5 million bags Group II coffee and 3.9 million to 4.4 million bags conillon, Unicafe said. Unicafe estimated that domestic consumption in calendar year 1997 should be 11 million bags, unchanged from 1996.

COLOMBIA - According to John Naranjo, commercial manager of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation, output in 1996/97 could drop as low as 10.4 million 60-kg bags, from 12.9 million bags in 1995/96. Federation officials have said unusually heavy rains during last months flowering period, and an increase in production costs, were among factors weighing on output during the current coffee year. Colombia intends to draw on federation stock, Naranjo said, adding that the majority of the 6 million bags of green coffee in federation inventories was in excellent condition. Jose Cardenas, the chief of the Colombia's National Growers' Federation, said Colombia would seek to boost its annual coffee output to a 'traditional' level of about 13 million bags in the coming years. Meanwhile it was reported that Colombia on February 21 raised its internal coffee price to a record-high of 310,250 pesos per 125-kg load in a bid to bring is close into line with overseas prices. MEXICO - Mexico plans to boost its annual coffee output to a total of about 8 million 60-kg bags by 2000 from current output of 4.7 million bags, Ruben Castillo, the executive president of the Mexican Coffee Council said. He said the plan would focus not on increasing Mexico's total coffee acreage but on the provision of technical assistance for growers and a concerted, government-backed effort to improve existing plantations. Because of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) Mexico was in a strategic position to take advantage of a market demanding up to 21 million 60-kg bags of coffee a year, he added. NAFTA also ruled out any chance that Mexico would eventually join in export retention schemes aimed at driving up world prices, he added.

UNITED STATES - US certified coffee stocks rose by 3,500 bags during the period from February 18 to February 20 to 24,295 bags. While stocks in New York, San Francisco and Miami remained unchanged, stocks in New Orleans rose by 3,500 bags to 8,001 bags (4,501 bags).

UNITED STATES - Coffee roastings for the week ended February 15 totalled approximately 300,000 60-kg bags, down from 425,000 bags in the previous week and compared with 300,000 bags in the corresponding period a year ago. Cumulative roastings totalled 2.590 million bags versus 2.520 million bags the same year ago period.
